title: The machine that changed everything
text: By 1450 a skilled scribe could copy perhaps two books a year, and a single volume could cost as much as a house. Within fifty years of Gutenberg's press, European printers had {{1}} some twenty million volumes — more than all the scribes of the preceding millennium had managed. The consequences went far beyond cheap reading. Uniform editions meant that scholars in Krakow and Oxford could argue about exactly the same text, and the copying errors that used to {{2}} into hand-copied pages simply stopped. Diagrams could now {{3}} far more widely than any lecturer's blackboard. Print standardised spelling, quietly {{4}} languages into their modern shapes, and turned scattered readers into a public following the same debates. The Reformation is hard to imagine without it: Luther's pamphlets sold hundreds of thousands of copies, {{5}} the authorities' ability to respond. Discoveries could {{6}} the accumulated work of predecessors with a precision unavailable to manuscript culture, and print also {{7}} the index, the page number and the title page — small inventions that made a book something you could cite. Historians still argue whether printing created the modern world or merely {{8}} it along; what is not disputed is that the flood of print has never receded.

gaps.explanation: 'printers had produced twenty million volumes' — manufactured them; proceed = go ahead, profess = claim, prolong = lengthen.
'errors that used to creep into hand-copied pages' — slip in unnoticed; 'errors creep in' is the fixed idiom.
'diagrams could now travel far more widely' — reach far-off places; trickle suggests a thin, slow flow, which contradicts the point.
'quietly nudging languages into their modern shapes' — gently pushing; nag pesters, and wave and fold do not fit the shaping image.
'sold copies, outpacing the authorities' ability to respond' — faster than they could act; outlast = survive longer than, outdo = beat at something.
'could draw on the accumulated work of predecessors' — use it as a resource; drag on = last tediously, which does not fit.
'print also popularised the index and the page number' — spread their use; populate = fill with people, postpone = delay.
'merely hurried it along' — accelerated it; haggle = argue over price, halve = cut by half.
